name: Grays Peak and Torreys Peak
region: Front Range, Arapaho and Pike National Forests

legs.route: Southeast ridge from the Grays-Torreys saddle
legs.connect: Drop down Grays' north ridge to the saddle at roughly 13,700 ft, then climb the broad southeast ridge of Torreys.

how: Take the Grays trail up the gulch and switchback the north slope to the top of Grays, which is the higher summit. From there the ridge descends gently north to a saddle, and a plain ridge walk leads up Torreys. The whole outing is non-technical walking, so the link adds only a few hundred feet of extra climbing and about an hour compared with Grays alone. Torreys is also reachable by the harder Kelso Ridge, a class 3 scramble that stands in for this ridge walk.
descent: Retrace to the saddle, then follow the trail that contours left across Grays' north side to rejoin the Grays trail near 13,200 ft, avoiding a second summit of Grays. Walk the standard trail to the trailhead.
logistics: Start from the trailhead at about 11,280 ft up a rough forest road; low-clearance cars park lower and walk. Roughly 8 miles and 3,600 ft round trip. Summer is the main window, and an early start keeps you off the tops before afternoon storms. In winter, avalanche slopes on Kelso Mountain can run over the approach.
notes: Sources agree on the saddle and descent. The Kelso Ridge page was read only for the Torreys alternative and the saddle descent; its combination with Grays is not described there, so no Kelso-plus-Grays link-up entry was written. Other pages: SummitPost pages returned 403.

name: DeCaLiBron (Democrat, Cameron, Lincoln, Bross)

legs.route: East slope from the cirque basin
Ridge walk (not an official separate summit)
legs.connect: Follow the connecting ridge north-east to the flat-topped Cameron without dropping far.
Continue along the same high ridge to the summit of Lincoln.

legs.route: Ridge from Lincoln; summit access restricted
legs.connect: Descend the ridge toward the Lincoln-Bross saddle; the summit itself sits on land that has been closed, so many parties skip it and loop back.

how: Climbers circle the cirque above the trailhead, taking the summits in sequence along a high ridge with only modest dips between them. Everything is class 2 tundra and talus, so the outing is about stamina and weather rather than skill. Cameron is usually a pass-through on the ridge rather than a separate climb.
descent: Return from the last point reached down a slope or trail back to the cirque basin and the trailhead, completing a loop rather than backtracking over the peaks.
logistics: The loop is about 7 miles and 3,500 ft. Parking is at the high trailhead and a daily fee applies. The road to it has been closed at times for construction, and private land around Bross means the summit may be off limits; check current land-manager notices before going.
notes: 14ers.com lists the combo at class 2, 3,500 ft, 7.5 mi; the other page lists 7.1 mi and 3,322 ft and says the Bross summit is closed and bypassed. Hoodline (July 2026) reports a Forest Service closure of the access road from June 4 to July 31, 2026. Bross leg flagged as optional/restricted.

name: Belford, Oxford and Missouri

legs.connect: Walk the obvious ridge south-west from Belford's summit, losing a modest amount of height before the climb.

legs.route: Standard northwest ridge via the pass
legs.connect: Backtrack toward Belford, or drop to the tundra saddle between Belford and Missouri, then climb Missouri by its normal ridge.

how: Belford and Oxford form a pair joined by a tundra ridge, and many parties stop there. Adding Missouri means leaving the ridge for the saddle toward Missouri, then climbing its northwest ridge and descending the standard way. The direct east ridge of Missouri from the pass is loose and rotten and best avoided. All three summits are class 2, but the day carries huge total gain.
descent: After Missouri, descend its standard route into the gulch and walk back down the road or trail to the car. Many parties cross Belford twice in this order.
logistics: Roughly 15 miles and 7,600 ft round trip from the gulch trailhead. Start before dawn and be off the ridges by early afternoon; the long approach road and a creek crossing add effort.
notes: Belford-Oxford-Missouri is the common order, though some do Missouri first. All three sources are 14ers.com pages.

name: Harvard-Columbia Traverse

legs.route: Standard trail then the south slopes

legs.connect: Follow the high ridge south-east, dropping into the basin and re-climbing around 1,500 ft over boulders to Columbia's summit.

how: The two highest peaks are tied by a ridge about 2.75 miles long that includes a big loss and regain of height over talus. Most parties go Harvard first and Columbia second. A bypass hugging the ridge crest adds class 3 scrambling for those who want to stay high. Cairns are sparse, so navigation matters more than technical skill.
descent: From Columbia, descend its slopes by the trail back to the trailhead, so the outing ends as a loop rather than a retrace.
logistics: About 15 miles and 6,000 ft round trip. Many parties base in the Horn Fork basin so each day is shorter. Start early; the boulder fields are slow and the traverse takes several hours.
notes: 14ers.com rates the traverse class 2; Mountain Project's crest bypass is third class (keep higher in the route text above). Direction: standard is Harvard to Columbia.

name: Bierstadt-Sawtooth-Evans Traverse

legs.connect: Descend Bierstadt's west ridge to the saddle, cross the Sawtooth ridge past the big gendarme, then follow a talus ramp and easy terrain to Evans.

how: Most parties climb Bierstadt first, drop to the low saddle, then work along the jagged ridge of the Sawtooth to Evans. The ridge is class 3 when kept on route and can turn to low fifth class if you stray, with the hardest ground near a large gendarme. Steep drops fall away on the west side. Snow on the ridge or saddle adds difficulty.
descent: Descend a gully back toward the pass and cross a boggy stretch to the parking area, instead of retracing the ridge.
logistics: Starts at the high pass on a dirt road; allow washboard time. About 10 hours for a typical party. Carry an ice axe if snow lingers. Wait for dry rock and calm weather.
notes: Both pages agree on the Bierstadt-first order and class 3 difficulty; a trip report mentions a fatal fall on the ridge. The 14ers.com route page for the Sawtooth was not read.

name: Redcloud and Sunshine

legs.connect: Walk the connecting ridge south, losing a few hundred feet to the saddle, then climb to Sunshine and return over Redcloud or take the Sundog loop.

how: Climbers go up Redcloud first, then follow the ridge down and across to Sunshine. Both are class 2. Returning over Redcloud means re-gaining a few hundred feet; others make a loop over a smaller bump called Sundog, which is preferably climbed rather than descended. The direct drop from the saddle toward the northwest face is loose and cliffy and not recommended.
descent: Either retrace over Redcloud and down its northeast ridge, or complete the loop via Sundog back to the trailhead.
logistics: Trailhead at about 10,400 ft; the road is washboarded but passable. Expect roughly 11 to 12 miles with about 4,800 ft of gain. Start early in summer. Handies Peak is usually saved for a separate day.
notes: Both are 14ers.com pages. The Sundog loop distance (about 9 mi, 4,450 ft) appeared only in a search summary of a SummitPost page, not read, so it is omitted from the text.

name: Bells Traverse (Maroon Peak to North Maroon Peak)

legs.route: Bells Traverse, then northeast ridge descent
legs.connect: Go north along the summit ridge, drop on the east side to the Bell Cord couloir notch, then climb the cliff bands and a final broken face to North Maroon.

how: Most parties go south to north, starting with Maroon Peak's south ridge. After a descent to the Bell Cord notch, the way goes over a series of cliff bands with low fifth-class moves, then loose ledges to North Maroon. Rock is loose, so test every hold. After the notch you are committed to North Maroon. A rope and nuts are optional for sections.
descent: Descend North Maroon via its northeast ridge, a fourth-class route marked by cairns, instead of retracing the traverse.
logistics: About 9.5 miles and 4,850 ft from the lake trailhead at 9,590 ft. Cars are barred past the entrance station during daytime summer hours, so plan parking early. Wilderness rules apply. Closures after accidents have occurred; check status.
notes: 14ers.com rates class 5; Mountain Project rates 5.2, noting others call it up to 5.4-5.7. Both give the NE ridge descent. Direction debated; south-to-north is described.

name: Crestone Traverse (Crestone Peak to Crestone Needle)
region: Sangre de Cristo Range, Sangre de Cristo Wilderness

legs.connect: From Crestone Peak, descend to about 13,650 ft, follow cairns across the ledges and gullies below the ridge, and finish up the Needle's steep summit wall.

duration: 1 long day or overnight at South Colony
how: The usual order is Peak first, then Needle. The connection stays below the crest through a series of red gullies and ribs, under a dark gendarme, then up a class 4 headwall. A 5.2 bulge adds to the difficulty. Going Needle to Peak is possible but typically means rappelling the headwall. Rope is optional; many solo, but a fall on the headwall is likely fatal.
descent: Descend the Needle by its standard south face route, which is shorter than the Peak's descent.
logistics: Trailhead at South Colony Lakes; the access road is rough and a four-wheel-drive vehicle helps. Around 13 miles and 7,000 ft from the upper trailhead. Wilderness rules apply; dry rock and calm wind are needed for the headwall.
notes: 14ers.com says class 5; Mountain Project says easy 5th and one of the Four Great 14er Traverses. Direction preference differs: MP recommends Peak to Needle; 14ers.com recommends Needle to Peak with a rappel.

name: El Diente - Mount Wilson Traverse
region: San Juan Mountains, Lizard Head Wilderness

legs.route: Ridge traverse over West Wilson, then Wilson's summit blocks
legs.connect: Follow the high ridge east for about a mile, bypassing the Organ Pipes and keeping to the right, then cross a loose wall and a short chimney to Wilson.

how: Climbers typically go El Diente first, then cross to Wilson. The ridge is class 4, with loose steep rock, a short exposed chimney, and cairns that help. Some bypass the Pin Point tower on its south side. Bailouts exist into Kilpacker Basin. A helmet is essential.
descent: Descend Wilson's southwest slopes to Kilpacker Basin, or use the north slopes to return to Navajo Basin. The slopes are loose scree.
logistics: From Kilpacker at about 9,350 ft the outing is roughly 13 miles and 4,800 ft. Reach the trailhead over a dirt road. Snow lingers into summer; crampons and an axe may be needed.
notes: 14ers.com rates class 4; Hiking Project calls it a loose, exposed class 4-5 traverse. Higher grade kept. SummitPost page returned 403. The Wilson Peak third 14er is not part of this traverse.

name: Blanca Peak and Ellingwood Point
region: Sangre de Cristo Range, Sierra Blanca

legs.route: Ridge from the saddle, then south face descent
legs.connect: From Blanca, drop to the high saddle near 13,800 ft and follow the ridge over a small notch to Ellingwood.

how: Most parties climb Blanca first, then descend the trail to the high saddle without losing the full height of the basin. A short ridge section links the two. Both standard routes are on the upper limit of class 2, and the link is class 3. Rockfall and a few notches are the main hazards.
descent: Come down Ellingwood's south face to the Lake Como road and trail, instead of retracing over Blanca.
logistics: A brutal four-wheel-drive road leads toward the lake; others park lower and walk a long way. About 18 miles and 6,800 ft round trip. Many camp at the lake to shorten the day. Bears and rodents raid camps; secure food.
notes: Both are 14ers.com pages. The trip report covers the Blanca to Ellingwood link in about an hour.

name: Little Bear - Blanca - Ellingwood Traverse
region: Sangre de Cristo Range, Sierra Blanca

legs.connect: Cross the mile-long knife-edge ridge east, passing over several towers and catwalks, to Blanca.

legs.route: Ridge from the Blanca-Ellingwood saddle, then south face descent
legs.connect: From Blanca, drop to the saddle and follow the ridge to Ellingwood.

duration: 1 very long day from a high camp
how: Little Bear's Hourglass is a steep class 4 choke with real rockfall, so a dawn start and helmet are standard. The connecting ridge to Blanca is very exposed, with towers, catwalks and a tricky downclimb; rated class 5 as a combination. Blanca to Ellingwood is a simpler ridge. Strong route-finding is needed.
descent: Descend Ellingwood's south face toward the lake rather than retracing the ridge.
logistics: Camp near the lake to shorten the day; the loop takes about eight hours from camp. The access road is rough. About 17 miles and 8,000 ft for Little Bear plus Blanca. Weather can turn fast.
notes: 14ers.com calls the ridge class 4 but the combo class 5; higher kept. Both pages are 14ers.com. The Ellingwood addition is documented only in the trip report.

name: Chicago Basin Peaks (Eolus, North Eolus, Windom, Sunlight)

legs.connect: Short optional side climb from Eolus.

how: Four summits are climbed from a single camp in the high basin. Each uses its own route, and several can be combined in one long day by strong parties. The technical ones (Eolus, Sunlight) are class 3 to 4 and are best done first; Windom's class 3 ridge is the easiest.
descent: Return to camp by each peak's own route, then hike out to the pickup point.
logistics: Many take the scenic railroad to the drop-off, avoiding a long approach hike; a basin camp lies near 11,200 ft. Check wilderness rules and plan for lingering snow in early summer.
notes: Only route classes and the base-camp role were confirmed from read pages. Direct connections between peaks and the permit rules were not confirmed; SummitPost 403 and AllTrails details were search snippets only.
